Greyfield sites are previously developed sites with at least 50% impervious surface area. Infill sites are vacant or underutilised lots of land, served by existing physical installations such as roads, power lines, sewer and water. The scope of controlled lots includes all lots owned or contractually available for ownership through option contracts or equivalent. The scope of homes includes single-family dwelling units, whether detached, attached or part of multi-family buildings. Reporting on these sites provides a metric for 'smart growth' strategies that help ensure compliance with environmental laws and mitigate financial risks associated with greenfield development, while potentially improving future growth opportunities through community approval.
summary: Requires disclosure of lots and homes on previously developed land (brownfield/greyfield) to evaluate 'smart growth' and environmental risk management strategies.
tags: brownfield, infill, smart growth, redevelopment

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its gross global Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to the atmosphere of the seven GHGs covered under the Kyoto Protocol—carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3). Emissions of all GHGs shall be consolidated and disclosed in metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-e) and calculated in accordance with published 100-year time horizon global warming potential (GWP) values. Gross emissions are GHGs emitted into the atmosphere before accounting for offsets, credits or other similar mechanisms that have reduced or compensated for emissions. Scope 1 emissions are defined and shall be calculated according to the methodology contained in The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (GHG Protocol). GHG emissions data shall be consolidated and disclosed according to the approach with which the entity consolidates its financial reporting data, which generally is aligned with the ‘financial control’ approach defined by the GHG Protocol.,,,
summary: Defines the mandatory scope and calculation methodology for reporting gross global Scope 1 GHG emissions using the GHG Protocol financial control approach.
tags: carbon footprint, ghg protocol, climate, reporting

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its long- and short-term strategy or plan to manage its Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The entity shall discuss its emission reduction target(s) and analyse its performance against the target(s), including, if relevant: the scope of the emission reduction target; whether the target is absolute or intensity-based; the percentage reduction against the base year; the time lines for the reduction activity, including the start year, the target year and the base year; the mechanism(s) for achieving the target; and any circumstances in which the target or base year emissions have been recalculated retrospectively. The entity shall discuss the activities and investments required to achieve the plans or targets, and any risks or limiting factors that might affect achievement. Relevant activities and investments may include: route optimisation, use of alternative fuels and energy sources, system improvements, optimisation of ship operation, improving efficiency through ship design and propulsion systems, and upgrading the fleet with new ships.,,,
summary: Mandates disclosure of emission reduction strategies and targets, including specific operational investments like route optimization and alternative fuels.
tags: strategy, targets, carbon reduction, ship design

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total amount of energy it consumed as an aggregate figure, in gigajoules (GJ). The scope of energy consumption includes energy from all sources, including energy purchased from external sources and energy produced by the entity itself (self-generated). For example, direct fuel usage, purchased electricity, and heating, cooling and steam energy are all included within the scope of energy consumption. The scope of energy consumption includes only energy directly consumed by the entity during the reporting period. In calculating energy consumption from fuels and biofuels, the entity shall use higher heating values (HHV), also known as gross calorific values (GCV), which are measured directly or taken from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). The entity shall also disclose the percentage of energy it consumed that was supplied from heavy fuel oil, defined as heavier oils that remain after distillate fuel oils and lighter hydrocarbons are distilled away in refinery operations.,,
summary: Establishes requirements for reporting total energy consumption and the specific percentage of energy derived from heavy fuel oil (bunker fuel).
tags: energy consumption, heavy fuel oil, bunker fuel, gcv

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of energy it consumed that is renewable energy. Renewable energy is defined as energy from sources that are replenished at a rate greater than or equal to their rate of depletion. The scope of renewable energy includes renewable fuel consumed, renewable energy produced and renewable energy purchased, if purchased through a renewable power purchase agreement (PPA) that explicitly includes renewable energy certificates (RECs) or Guarantees of Origin (GOs). For any renewable electricity generated on-site, any RECs and GOs shall be retained and retired or cancelled on behalf of the entity. For renewable PPAs and green power products, the agreement shall explicitly include and convey that RECs and GOs be retained or replaced and retired or cancelled on behalf of the entity for the entity to claim them as renewable energy. The scope of renewable energy from biomass sources is limited to materials certified to a third-party standard such as FSC, SFI, PEFC or American Tree Farm System.,,,
summary: Outlines strict verification and certification requirements for renewable energy claims, including the retention and retirement of RECs and GOs.
tags: renewable energy, recs, certifications, ppa

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its emissions of air pollutants, in metric tonnes per pollutant, released into the atmosphere. The scope of the disclosure includes air pollutants associated with the entity’s direct air emissions resulting from all the entity’s activities and sources of emissions, which may include stationary or mobile sources, production facilities, office buildings and transportation fleets. The entity shall disclose its emissions of (1) oxides of nitrogen (NOx), reported as NOx (excluding N2O); (2) oxides of sulphur (SOx), reported as SOx; and (3) particulate matter 10 micrometres or less in diameter (PM10), reported as PM10. PM10 is defined as any airborne finely divided solid or liquid material with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 10 micrometres. The entity may discuss the calculation method for its emissions disclosure, such as whether data is from continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS), engineering calculations or mass balance calculations.,,
summary: Requires standardized reporting of localized air pollutants (NOx, SOx, PM10) which are critical environmental externalities for port-side operations.
tags: nox, sox, particulate matter, air quality

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the shipping duration spent in marine protected areas or areas with protected conservation status. Shipping duration is the sum of the travel days (24-hour periods or fractions thereof), including time spent docked at ports. A marine protected area is defined as any area of the intertidal or subtidal terrain reserved by law to protect the environment, including Areas to be Avoided, Areas with Mandatory Ship Reporting Systems, and Emission Control Areas (ECAs) under MARPOL Annex VI. Areas of protected conservation status include Biosphere Reserves recognized by UNESCO, IUCN Protected Areas (categories I–VI), marine sanctuaries, national parks, and Marine Natura 2000 sites. The entity may discuss its shipping activities in areas that have no official designation but that present high biodiversity or ecosystem services risks. This metric identifies exposure to ecologically sensitive zones where unregulated discharges or accidents could result in significant legal and environmental consequences.,,,,,
summary: Mandates tracking of operational time in ecologically sensitive and protected areas to assess risks to biodiversity and potential regulatory violations.
tags: marine protected areas, biodiversity, marpol, biodiversity risk

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of its fleet that has implemented ballast water treatment. Ballast water treatment includes implementation of an integrated system of ballast water treatment equipment that is approved by the applicable jurisdictional legal or regulatory authority to meet the performance criteria in D2 standard of the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Ballast Water Management (BWM) convention. Approved systems must discharge less than 10 viable organisms per cubic metre that are greater than or equal to 50 micrometres and less than 10 viable organisms per millilitre that are less than 50 micrometres but greater than or equal to 10 micrometres. The percentage shall be calculated as the number of ships in the entity’s fleet that have implemented ballast water treatment systems that meet the D2 standard specifications divided by the total number of ships in the fleet. Compliance with these international regulations often requires significant capital expenditures to upgrade waste management systems.,,
summary: Requires reporting on fleet compliance with the IMO D2 standard for ballast water treatment to mitigate the risk of introducing invasive species.
tags: ballast water, imo, d2 standard, water pollution

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total number of spills and releases of hazardous material to the environment and (2) the total volume of spills and releases in cubic metres. Spills and releases include releases overboard that are intentional or accidental, including those resulting from sabotage, leakage over time, or events outside of operational control. The scope includes hazardous materials (explosives, toxic, oxidizing or corrosive materials) in reportable quantities, noxious liquid substances (Category X or Y) according to MARPOL Annex II, and oils. The volume shall be calculated as the total estimated amount spilled that reached the environment, without reducing that figure by the amount of such material subsequently recovered, evaporated or otherwise lost. The entity may provide a disaggregation of spills and releases by type and by their proximity to land, such as those 24 nautical miles or closer to shore. Illegal dumping or unregulated discharges can result in hefty fines and damage to the supplier's risk profile.,,,,
summary: Mandates disclosure of the frequency and volume of hazardous spills and oil releases, which directly impacts a supplier's operational risk profile.
tags: hazardous materials, oil spills, marpol, environmental risk

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its lost time incident rate (LTIR) for work-related injuries and illnesses. A lost time incident is defined as an incident that results in absence from work beyond the date or shift when it occurred. The rate shall be calculated as: (lost time incidents) / (1,000,000 hours worked). The scope of the disclosure includes all employees regardless of employee location, including direct and contract employees who work aboard the entity’s vessels. The International Safety Management Code (ISM Code) provides additional guidance in implementing lost time incident reporting. Health and safety risks are particularly acute during loading and unloading at ports where ships must operate on tight schedules, increasing injury risk and fatigue. Entities with inadequate safety management systems may witness increased employee turnover and worker-related expenses, including medical insurance premiums and worker pay-outs.,,,
summary: Sets a standardized benchmark for workforce safety, requiring the reporting of injury-related work absences for both direct and contracted crew members.
tags: ltir, workforce safety, ism code, maritime labor

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total amount of monetary losses incurred during the reporting period resulting from legal proceedings associated with bribery, corruption or other unethical business practices. The legal proceedings shall include any adjudicative proceeding involving the entity, whether before a court, a regulator, an arbitrator or otherwise. The losses shall include all monetary liabilities to the opposing party or to others (settlements, fines, etc.) resulting from civil, regulatory, or criminal actions. The entity shall briefly describe the nature (e.g., guilty plea, deferred agreement) and context (e.g., bribery or facilitation payment) of all monetary losses and describe any corrective actions implemented in response. This may include specific changes in operations, management, processes, business partners, training or technology. Port facilitation payments are considered standard in some countries, but enforcement of anti-bribery laws may result in significant one-time costs and affect an entity’s social licence to operate.,,,
summary: Requires disclosure of financial penalties for corruption and a description of the resulting operational changes, highlighting risks in countries prone to facilitation payments.
tags: bribery, corruption, legal losses, ethics

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total number of marine casualties involving its fleet and the percentage classified as very serious. A marine casualty is defined as an event in connection with ship operations resulting in: death or serious injury; loss of a person from a ship; material damage to the ship or marine infrastructure; or severe damage to the environment. A very serious marine casualty involves the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. The entity shall describe marine casualties and very serious marine casualties, including root causes, outcomes and any corrective actions implemented in response. Accidents or leaks involving large vessels can have significant impacts on life, property and the environment, often leading to negative media attention and significant clean-up costs that impair an entity’s finances.,,,
summary: Mandates the reporting of marine accidents and the implementation of corrective actions, which are critical for evaluating a supplier's safety and environmental management.
tags: marine casualty, safety, environment, corrective action

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total number of Conditions of Class or Recommendations received from a flag administration or a recognised organisation (RO). Conditions of Class or Recommendations are requirements imposed by an administration (or delegate such as a classification society) to be carried out within a specific time limit to retain vessel class. These include repairs or renewals related to damages that affect classification (e.g., grounding, structural damages, machinery damages), supplementary survey requirements, and temporary repairs. The scope of the disclosure includes all Conditions of Class regardless of whether they resulted in withdrawal, suspension or invalidation of a vessel’s class certificate. These periodic dry-docking maintenance periods and annual class-renewal surveys are essential safety measures used to reduce the risk of accidents in the global shipping industry.,,,
summary: Establishes a metric for vessel maintenance and safety compliance based on formal requirements from classification societies or flag administrations.
tags: vessel class, maintenance, safety audits, repairs

doc_title: Marine Transportation Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total number of deficiencies and (2) the total number of detentions it received from regional port state control (PSC) organisations. A deficiency is a condition found non-compliant with the requirements of conventions such as MARPOL, SOLAS, STCW, or the ILO Maritime Labour Convention. A detention is an intervention action taken if the condition of a ship or its crew does not substantially adhere to applicable conventions, ensuring the ship will not sail until it can proceed without presenting a danger to persons or the environment. The scope includes deficiencies and detentions issued by PSC organisations that are signatories to regional memoranda of understanding (MoU). These metrics serve as high-strength indicators of a supplier's compliance with international safety, environmental, and labor standards.,,,
summary: Standardizes reporting of port state control interventions, which act as a critical external validation of a supplier's adherence to international maritime law.
tags: port state control, deficiencies, detentions, maritime law

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its approach to identifying information system vulnerabilities that may pose a data security risk. Data security risk is defined as the risk of any circumstance or event with the potential to affect organisational operations, assets, individuals, or governments through an information system via unauthorised access, destruction, disclosure, modification of information, or denial of service. The entity shall describe its approach to managing identified risks and vulnerabilities, which may include operational procedures, management processes, structure of products, selection of business partners, employee training and use of technology. The entity may describe the degree to which its approach is aligned with an external standard or framework for managing data security, such as the ISO/IEC 27000-series or the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity.
summary: Requires suppliers to disclose their methodologies for identifying and managing cybersecurity vulnerabilities, including alignment with standards like ISO 27001 or NIST.
tags: cybersecurity, vulnerability, iso 27001, risk management

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe the nature, scope and implementation of its policies and practices related to customer privacy, with a specific focus on how it manages the collection, use and retention of customer information, including demographic data, confidential business information and personal data. Customer information includes records of communications, content of communications, demographic data, personally identifiable information or confidential business information. Demographic data includes gender, age, ethnicity, language, disabilities, mobility, home ownership and employment status. Confidential business information concerns trade secrets, processes, operations, or other information of commercial value, the disclosure of which is likely to cause substantial harm to the competitive position of the person or entity from which the information was obtained. Personal data is defined as any information that relates to an identified or identifiable living individual.
summary: Mandates disclosure of policies regarding the collection and protection of customer information, including demographic and confidential business data.
tags: data privacy, personal data, confidential information, compliance

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe the information ‘lifecycle’ (collection, use, retention, processing, disclosure and destruction of information) and how information-handling practices at each stage may affect individuals’ privacy. With respect to data collection, the entity may discuss the data or types of data it collects without the consent of an individual, data that requires opt-in consent and data that requires an opt-out action from the individual. With respect to data usage, the entity may discuss the data or types of data used internally, and under which circumstances the entity shares, sells, rents or otherwise distributes data or information to third parties. With respect to data retention, the entity may discuss the data or types of data it retains, the duration of retention and what practices ensure that data is stored securely. This includes the destruction of information once it is no longer required.
summary: Outlines the expectation for suppliers to detail their data management lifecycle, including consent mechanisms and third-party data sharing.
tags: data retention, consent, data processing, third-party sharing

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its use of privacy impact assessments (PIAs) or data protection impact assessments (DPIAs). A PIA or DPIA is an analysis of how information is handled that ensures handling conforms to applicable legal, regulatory and policy requirements regarding privacy. These assessments determine the risks and effects of collecting, maintaining and disseminating information in identifiable form in an electronic information system. Furthermore, PIAs and DPIAs examine and evaluate protections and alternative processes for handling information to mitigate potential privacy risks. The entity’s disclosure shall be sufficient such that it is specific to the risks the entity faces, but disclosure itself would not compromise the entity’s ability to maintain data privacy and security. These assessments are critical for identifying and mitigating potential privacy risks before they lead to breaches.
summary: Specifies the requirement for using formal privacy and data protection impact assessments to identify and mitigate information handling risks.
tags: pia, dpia, privacy risk, risk assessment

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total number of data breaches identified during the reporting period, including the percentage that involve customers’ confidential business information and personal data breaches. A data breach is defined as an unauthorised occurrence that jeopardises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of an entity’s information systems. The entity shall describe any corrective actions taken in response to data breaches, such as changes in operations, management, processes, products, business partners, training or technology. The scope includes incidents during which encrypted data was acquired with an encryption key that also was acquired. The entity may also disclose its policy for disclosing data breaches to affected customers in a timely manner. Data breaches may compromise client perception and adversely affect an entity’s ability to attract and retain clients.
summary: Requires reporting on the frequency of data breaches and the specific corrective actions implemented to address systemic security or process failures.
tags: data breach, corrective action, security incident, disclosure

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of gender representation and diversity group representation among its employees for executive management, non-executive management and all other employees. Executive management is defined as chief executives and senior officials who formulate and review the entity’s policies and plan overall activities. Diversity is defined as the presence of people from populations who have been underrepresented in a particular field or are otherwise historically marginalised. Diversity groups may be defined by dimensions such as race, ethnicity, disability status, region of origin, migrant status, indigenous background, age, socioeconomic background, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity. The entity shall calculate the percentage for each employee category as the number of employees in each group divided by the total number of employees in the respective employee category.
summary: Standardizes the quantitative reporting of workforce diversity and gender representation across all organizational levels from executive to general staff.
tags: diversity, gender, representation, human capital

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its policies and programmes for fostering equitable employee representation in its global operations. Relevant policies may include maintaining transparency of hiring, promotion and wage practices, ensuring equal employment opportunities, developing and disseminating diversity policies, and ensuring management accountability for equitable representation. Relevant programmes may include training on diversity, mentorship and sponsorship programmes, partnership with employee resource and advisory groups, and provision of flexible work schedules to accommodate the varying needs of employees. Enhancing workforce diversity, particularly among management positions, helps entities attract and develop the best talent. These disclosures provide insight into an entity's commitment to building a workforce that reflects its markets and contributes to increased productivity and performance through all levels of the entity.
summary: Mandates disclosure of specific DEI policies and programs, including hiring transparency, mentorship, and management accountability for equitable representation.
tags: recruitment, mentorship, training, inclusion

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose employee engagement as a percentage, calculated based on the results of an employee engagement survey or research study conducted by the entity or an external party. The percentage shall be calculated as the number of employees who self-describe as actively engaged divided by the total number of employees who completed the survey. The entity shall briefly describe the source of its survey, the method used to calculate the percentage, and a summary of questions or statements included, such as those related to goal-setting, support to achieve goals, training and development, work processes, and commitment to the organisation. If results are limited to a subset of employees, the entity shall provide the percentage of employees included and the representativeness of the sample to ensure data integrity.
summary: Sets a benchmark for measuring and disclosing employee engagement levels using standardized survey methodologies and representative sampling.
tags: survey, engagement rate, workforce, human capital

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its policies to ensure professional integrity, including aspects relating to conflict of interest, accuracy of data and corruption. The scope includes policies, training and implementation of codes of ethics as well as investigations, enforcement and disciplinary procedures relating to: avoidance of conflicts of interest; oversight of advisory services; maintenance and reporting of accurate data; protection of confidential business information; prevention of billing fraud; avoidance of corruption including whistle-blower protection; privacy guidelines and security clearances; employee training on relevant regulations; mechanisms for internal reporting about violations; processes for internal investigations of malpractice or negligence; and disciplinary actions for violations of professional integrity policies. Maintaining high professional standards is essential for strengthening an entity’s licence to operate and for attracting and retaining clients.
summary: Outlines requirements for suppliers to disclose ethical management systems, focusing on data accuracy, anti-corruption, and conflict of interest mitigation.
tags: ethics, anti-corruption, conflict of interest, code of conduct

doc_title: Professional & Commercial Services Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total amount of monetary losses incurred during the reporting period resulting from legal proceedings associated with professional integrity, including negligence, malpractice, breach of contract, fraud, corruption and bribery. The legal proceedings shall include any adjudicative proceeding involving the entity, whether before a court, a regulator, or an arbitrator. Losses include all monetary liabilities to the opposing party (settlement, verdict, etc.), including fines and other monetary liabilities incurred from civil actions, regulatory proceedings and criminal actions. The entity shall briefly describe the nature and context of all monetary losses resulting from legal proceedings and describe any corrective actions implemented in response, such as specific changes in operations, management, processes, products, business partners, training or technology. These losses reflect risks to the entity’s professional standards and trust.
summary: Requires disclosure of financial penalties from integrity-related legal issues and the corresponding operational changes made to prevent future negligence or fraud.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: To reduce industry emissions effectively, companies must address their Scope 3 emissions. For those with the majority of emissions in the Scope 3 upstream category, this will require active engagement with their suppliers. With the exception of the cement and concrete and transport services industries, all of the listed sectors have the majority of their emissions stemming from Scope 3. SMEs and mid-sized companies play a significant role in the supply chain of many large corporations, making it essential for those aiming to reduce their carbon footprint to integrate SMEs and mid-sized suppliers into their decarbonization strategies. This makes active supplier engagement a necessity for enterprises seeking to meet net-zero targets.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: Improving access to accurate, real-time sustainability data is critical for businesses to set meaningful targets, track progress and respond to growing regulatory and customer expectations. Many SMEs and mid-sized manufacturers still face challenges in systematically gathering and using data related to their environmental impact. Building the capability for automated data collection is an important enabler, as the principle that "you cannot improve what you do not measure" remains particularly true in manufacturing. By integrating sensors, edge-layer controls and manufacturing software, businesses can automate data collection across almost any process, leading to improved production oversight and operational performance when deployed effectively. This involves monitoring key areas such as energy consumption, water use and raw material inputs at the process or site level.

chunk_text: The SME Climate Hub offers smaller firms a suite of free, user-friendly tools to help SMEs begin measuring their carbon emissions across Scopes 1, 2 and 3 in various scenarios and create annual GHG emissions reports with the tailored template originated from CDP's framework. This includes a Small Business Carbon Calculator for businesses with 1-50 employees at a single site and an Advanced Business Carbon Calculator for companies with multiple sites, providing a detailed and auditable emissions measurement tool. Additionally, a Scope 3 Specific Calculator converts procurement data into accurate Scope 3 emissions information, helping businesses address supply chain emissions. The SME Reporting Tool as a free online platform to enable smaller businesses to create annual climate reports, with a template tailored for them and originated from CDP's Climate Disclosure Framework.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: Building on the impact achieved and derived learnings from initial quick-win sustainability projects, organizations can shift to embedding sustainability in their overarching operational and corporate strategy. SMEs and mid-sized manufacturers can consider tackling longer-term high ROI initiatives that were previously set aside due to moderate-to-high complexity to address. Examples could include incorporating efficient design or "eco-design" principles into product development, or redefining procurement strategy and working with supply chain leads to identify additional suppliers that may be closer to the company facilities and could be integrated into the existing supply chain to increase operational resiliency and reduce emissions. These types of projects may take longer to execute and require the establishment of new processes or standard operating procedures, but they can lead to long-term value.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: Many large corporations are training smaller manufacturers in their supply chains on sustainable practices, focusing on energy efficiency, waste reduction and green technologies. Through collaboration, they help smaller manufacturers adopt eco-friendly operations, enhance cost savings and strengthen supply chains for a greener future. Schneider Electric launched the Zero Carbon Project in 2021 to help its top suppliers reduce operational emissions (Scope 1 and Scope 2) intensity by 50% by 2025 - a critical step towards its broader goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. Through training, digital tools and tailored support, the initiative helps suppliers measure emissions, set targets and implement reduction strategies. More than 1,000 suppliers have joined, achieving a 42% operational emissions intensity reduction by Q1 of 2025, with 70% assessing their carbon footprint for the first time.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: To establish an environmental sustainability programme effectively, manufacturers need to assess their starting point and build an understanding of sustainability principles and methodologies. In an ideal scenario, companies would train dedicated staff in the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol, the leading framework for corporate carbon accounting. In reality, limited time and resources often prevent smaller firms from forming full sustainability teams. Despite these challenges, such companies can designate a "sustainability lead" within their operations teams to receive targeted training on key environmental metrics and the basics of Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions. This role involves participating in training programmes and conducting self-assessments to identify key areas of improvement opportunity (e.g. energy use, water consumption) and setting sustainability goals and strategies to improve energy efficiency.

doc_title: Sustainability Meets Growth: A Roadmap for SMEs and Mid-Sized Manufacturers
chunk_text: Positive policy incentives can encourage smaller businesses to invest proactively in sustainable technologies, improve energy and resource efficiency and adopt cleaner production practices. The policy also promotes market-based incentives such as preferential government procurement for eco-friendly SMEs and facilitates their participation in carbon markets. By outlining climate ambition and policy trajectories in the short, medium and long terms, governments can design policies that are both effective and proportionate to the capacities of businesses of varying sizes, ensuring that sustainability becomes a driver of innovation.

chunk_text: Governments can provide financial assistance in the form of loan application support specialists. This type of support ensures that sustainability projects are presented in a manner that traditional financial institutions can evaluate and fund. doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Companies shall publicly report the following information: data for all seven GHGs (CO2​, CH4​, N2​O, SF6​, PFCs, HFCs and NF3​), disaggregated by GHG and reported in units of both metric tonnes and tonnes CO2​-equivalent (CO2​e). Total scope 1 and 2 emissions shall be reported without subtractions for trades in offsets. Additionally, companies shall report an outline of the operational boundaries chosen and, if scope 3 is included, a list specifying which types of scope 3 activities are covered. For non-mechanical sources, companies should provide a description of whether the calculation methodologies used are IPCC Tier 1, 2, or 3, and a description of how those methodologies were chosen based on specific quality criteria. A reference or link to the calculation methodologies used, providing a link to any calculation tools used, is also required to ensure transparency and consistency in the reported greenhouse gas flux data.
summary: Defines the mandatory quantitative and descriptive data points required for a compliant agricultural GHG inventory.

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Agricultural emissions will often form a substantial part of the scope 3 inventories of downstream companies, such as processors, brand manufacturers, and retailers. These emissions typically fall into the Scope 3 Standard's Category 1 (Purchased Goods and Services). Upstream companies, such as manufacturers of farm inputs like seeds and fertilizers, will find these emissions fall into Category 11 (Use of Sold Products). Companies completing a value chain assessment should consult the Scope 3 Standard for additional requirements and guidance on including agriculture in their inventories. Alternatively, producers may develop scope 1 and 2 inventories specifically to supply information requested by a buyer for the purpose of the buyer's own scope 3 and product inventories. This ensures that agricultural impacts are effectively integrated into the broader corporate value chain carbon accounting and helps identify products with significant GHG footprints based on raw material use.
summary: Explains how agricultural data serves the Scope 3 reporting needs of enterprise buyers in the food supply chain.
tags: scope 3, value chain, purchased goods, supplier disclosure

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: For the purposes of reporting under this Guidance, growers are assumed to retain operational control over the contracted production and should therefore account for 100% of the associated emissions under scope 1 or 2 using the operational control approach. Production contracts are distinct in that they are agreements between contractors (growers) and contractees (integrators) that cede some measure of control over the production process to the integrator. The contract specifies the services to be provided by the grower, such as fertilizer application schedules and husbandry conditions, and the manner in which the grower is to be compensated. In cases where the integrator has established multi-year contracts and provides extensive inputs, both integrators and growers should account for a portion of the emissions according to their share of investments in the production process under financial or equity share approaches. This helps define which entity is responsible for emissions in complex sourcing arrangements.
summary: Clarifies emissions ownership and reporting responsibility for contract farmers under different organizational boundary approaches.
tags: production contracts, operational control, sourcing, accountability

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: When high-quality activity data are not available for all of the emissions sources that need to be included in an inventory, companies should prioritize their data collection efforts based on source magnitude. Key sources are those that are expected to have the highest GHG fluxes, offer the most emissions reduction potential, and are most relevant to the company's business goals. The most rigorous approach to identifying key sources is to use quantitative data to rank the size of different sources and sinks. Companies should rank all sources from largest to smallest according to their estimated GHG fluxes and apply a pre-determined, percentage cumulative threshold (e.g., sources cumulatively responsible for 70% of GHG fluxes). Collecting higher quality data for these key sources allows companies to more effectively set reduction targets and track progress over time while making the most efficient use of available resources.
summary: Outlines the "Key Source" method for suppliers to prioritize data collection for the most significant emissions drivers.
tags: key sources, data quality, carbon accounting, prioritization

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: To ensure consistent tracking of GHG fluxes over time, the base period inventory shall be recalculated when changes occur to the inventory boundaries or process that would significantly impact the base inventory. These changes include structural changes that transfer ownership or control of operations, such as mergers, acquisitions, and divestments, as long as those operations existed in the base period. Recalculation is also required for changes in calculation methodologies, such as the use of improved emission factors, or the discovery of errors that are significant on their own or collectively. In determining whether changes are significant, companies should set significance thresholds (e.g., changes that cause a change exceeding x% of the base period inventory). Once defined, a significance threshold should be applied consistently over time to ensure that historical comparisons remain meaningful and the audit trail is preserved.
summary: Defines the mandatory conditions and thresholds for recalculating baseline emissions data to ensure year-over-year comparability.
tags: baseline, recalculation, mergers, data integrity, significance threshold

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Individual years will often not serve as representative base periods due to changes in environmental conditions beyond the control of the company, such as heat waves or atypical farming practices like clearing forest for production. In such cases, companies should average GHG flux data from multiple, consecutive years to form a more representative base period. In general, this Guidance recommends at least a three-year base period, which is often sufficient to smooth over inter-annual variability. Multi-year base periods are recommended for many companies because agricultural activities and environmental conditions that affect GHG fluxes can change significantly over time. Furthermore, the base period should not be an individual crop year or production season that is less than one year; otherwise, the effects of seasonal management activities, such as tillage or winter cover crops, may not be reflected in the base period inventory.
summary: Recommends using a three-year average for baselines to account for the high inter-annual variability in agricultural emissions.
tags: base year, multi-year average, variability, crop cycle

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Companies should account for historical changes in land use (LUC) that occur within a certain "look back" period prior to the base period. This look back period should be equal in length to the amortization period for the stock concerned (e.g., 20 years if the default IPCC amortization period for mineral soil organic stocks is used). Thus, if LUC happened within the 5 years preceding the base period, it is considered best practice to reflect it in the inventories for the base period and later reporting periods. When recalculating the base period inventory, new landowners should assess whether these changes occurred within the relevant look back period. If a company acquired land that had been deforested by the prior land-owner five years before the new land-owner's base period, the associated changes in C stocks should be included in the recalculated base period inventory. This ensures that historical impacts on carbon stocks are accurately reflected despite changes in ownership.
summary: Establishes a 20-year look-back requirement for land use changes to prevent suppliers from ignoring previous deforestation or land conversion.
tags: deforestation, land use change, historical luc, carbon stocks

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Amortizing the CO2​ fluxes from changes in carbon (C) stocks involves allocating these fluxes across time and multiple inventories to ensure the more consistent accounting of C stock impacts. When amortization is necessary, companies should use a linear-rate approach, wherein the total amount of CO2​ flux is amortized evenly over multiple inventories. This involves dividing the total flux by the number of years in the amortization period and reporting the quotient in each year. The length of the amortization period for woody biomass stocks should be the length of the nominal harvest or maturity cycle. In the absence of other information, companies may assume an amortization period of 20 years for dead organic matter stocks and the organic C stocks in mineral soils. If management shifts occur that would reverse any soil C sequestration that has previously been amortized, such as ceasing no-till practices, companies should record the cumulative gains as CO2​ emissions in that inventory period.
summary: Describes the requirement to spread carbon stock changes over 20 years to provide a realistic view of soil and biomass carbon impacts.
tags: amortization, soil carbon, sequestration, linear-rate, no-till

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Identification of uncertainty sources helps companies understand the level of confidence users should have in inventory results and estimates of emissions reductions. Parameter uncertainty is a measure of how close the data used to calculate the results (e.g., activity data and emission factors) are to the true actual data and GHG fluxes. Companies should identify and track key uncertainty sources throughout the inventory process and iteratively check whether the uncertainty is adequate for the company's business goals. Information on uncertainty should be reported in inventories through qualitative descriptions of uncertainty sources and quantitative representations such as error bars or probability density functions. If uncertainty bounds are asymmetrical, the larger uncertainty should be used to remain conservative. This reporting ensures transparency regarding the limitations of the calculation approaches and data quality used in the supplier's sustainability disclosures.
summary: Requires suppliers to disclose data uncertainty to ensure buyers can judge the reliability of reported carbon footprints.
tags: parameter uncertainty, data quality, risk, transparency

doc_title: GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance
chunk_text: Physical allocation of GHG emissions is preferred when a physical relationship amongst products can be established and this relationship drives their relative GHG impacts. This approach is also preferred when prices change significantly or frequently over time, as seen with commodity crop prices, or when prices are not well-correlated with underlying physical properties and GHG fluxes. For example, if mass is the main causal factor, allocations can be based on the mass of farm outputs. Economic allocation is preferred when a physical relationship cannot be established or adequately reflect GHG impacts, or when co-products were a waste output that acquires value in the market as a replacement for another material input, such as manure as a replacement for fertilizer. A single approach should be used consistently to allocate the GHG data for all products of a farm to prevent over- or under-counting of total farm-wide fluxes.
summary: Provides the rules for how suppliers should split emissions between different products (e.g., meat vs. leather, or grain vs. straw).
tags: allocation, co-products, economic allocation, physical allocation

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies reporting a corporate- or organization-level GHG inventory in conformance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol shall follow the Land Sector and Removals Standard and Guidance if the company has significant land sector activities in its operations or value chain and/or if the company chooses to account for and report CO2​ removals or CO2​ capture with geologic storage in the current year or has done so in previous years. Companies with land sector activities in their operations or value chain that do not follow and report in conformance with the Land Sector and Removals Standard and Guidance shall disclose and justify why those activities are not significant. This applies to companies that purchase, consume, process, or sell significant amounts of food, fiber, feed, bioenergy, or other agricultural products (e.g., food and beverage companies, consumer goods companies, retailers, or food service companies).,
summary: Defines the mandatory applicability of land sector reporting for any company with significant agricultural products in their value chain.
tags: land sector, applicability, ghg protocol, mandatory

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: To account for scope 3 emissions, removals, and other metrics, companies apply a scope 3 spatial boundary determined by the level of traceability they can establish to known lands or regions. To apply a sourcing region, LMU, or harvested area as the scope 3 spatial boundary... companies shall have physical traceability to the sourcing region, LMU, or harvested area within their value chain. If companies seek to demonstrate physical traceability for an activity and/or volume of product in their value chain, companies shall implement traceability systems (e.g., through certification programs or audited internal systems) that apply the following chain of custody models: Identity preservation; Segregation; Controlled blending; Mass balance... Companies cannot demonstrate physical traceability using book-and-claim approaches or those mass balance approaches where the volume of inputs and outputs with the specified characteristics is unknown or not specified.,,
summary: Establishes the requirement for physical traceability and specific chain-of-custody models to claim granular land-based emissions data.

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall account for LUC emissions that occurred within the LUC assessment period. For annual crops or other land-based products or services with a cultivation cycle or rotation period less than or equal to 20 years, the assessment period is 20 years. The LUC assessment period is prior to and includes the reporting year. For land-based products with a cultivation cycle or rotation period of more than 20 years, the length of that cycle or period is used as the LUC assessment period. Companies shall allocate the LUC emissions to each year in the LUC assessment period using linear discounting... products grown closer in time to the year of conversion are weighted more heavily than products grown more distant in time from the year of conversion. Companies shall use either a direct land use change (dLUC) or statistical land use change (sLUC) calculation approach for a given product type.,,,
summary: Mandates a 20-year look-back period for land use change, ensuring suppliers remain accountable for historical deforestation.
tags: land use change, assessment period, linear discounting, deforestation

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall account for and report scope 1 and scope 3 agricultural "land occupation" (in hectares). Land use, when measured in hectares, does not differentiate between different types of land or the ability of those lands to store carbon... Companies should go beyond reporting total scope 1 and scope 3 land occupation in hectares by disaggregating by land type: Separately report scope 1 and scope 3 agricultural land occupation in hectares by land use category (e.g., cropland, grassland) in the "land occupation" accounting subcategory under "land use." Additionally, they shall disclose in their GHG report the yields and factors used to calculate land occupation. This accounting category represents the amount of agricultural land occupied by the company for products it produces or sources, which helps to quantify a company's contribution to global land use and conversion pressure.,,,,
summary: Requires suppliers to report the physical area (hectares) required to produce the goods sourced by the buyer.
tags: land occupation, hectares, land pressure, yield

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall quantify land carbon leakage if any of the following activities occur in a company's operations or value chain in the reporting year: Use of food or other agricultural products for non-food, non-feed use (e.g., crop-based biofuels or bio-based feedstocks); Significant reduction in food production that occurs over the long-term, resulting from a change in land management or land use for which land management CO2​ removals are attributed; Significant reduction in crop yields per hectare that occurs over the long-term, resulting from a change in cropland management practices. Companies shall quantify land carbon leakage using the annualized, average carbon stock losses from the conversion of native ecosystems to agricultural land to replace the quantity and type of reduced or diverted food or feed production at average yields ("carbon opportunity cost"). This must be reported separately from the physical GHG inventory.,,,
summary: Requires suppliers to account for emissions caused by displacing food production, particularly relevant for bio-based material sourcing.
tags: carbon leakage, biofuels, carbon opportunity cost, biomass

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: All changes in land carbon stocks on productive agricultural land in the reporting year are considered anthropogenic. Companies shall fully account for all net land carbon stock losses on all agricultural lands in the reporting year, including changes due to degradation and carbon stock losses from fires, storms, and other natural disturbances. This requirement ensures only anthropogenic CO2​ emissions and removals are accounted for and addresses concerns with companies including large areas of non-productive lands. Land management net biogenic CO2​ emissions are calculated using a stock-change accounting approach. Companies are required to estimate the net land carbon stock change for all required carbon pools. If the net land carbon stock change decreases, the difference is accounted for as land management net CO2​ emissions.,,
summary: Establishes that all carbon losses on agricultural land, including from "natural" causes, must be reported as human-caused emissions.
tags: anthropogenic impacts, carbon stock, monitoring, degradation

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall disclose in their GHG report: For each scope, scope 3 category, and accounting subcategory, companies shall describe the methodologies, scope 3 allocation methods, and assumptions used to calculate emissions, removals, or other metrics; and types and sources of data (e.g., activity data, emissions factors, carbon opportunity cost factors, conversion factors, and GWP values). For each scope 3 category, companies shall disclose the percentage of emissions calculated using data obtained from suppliers or other value chain partners. Companies should prioritize using higher accuracy methods and reduce uncertainty as far as is practical. Companies should collect supplier-specific data for the GHG sources and sinks that are most significant (i.e., comprise the greatest share of the inventory) across their operations and value chain and improve their data collection over time by gathering more supplier-specific data and evaluating data quality.,,,
summary: Mandates disclosure of the percentage of primary supplier data used, serving as a key metric for supply chain transparency.
tags: supplier-specific data, data quality, disclosure, transparency

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: If companies account for and report removals in their GHG inventory, they shall adhere to the permanence principle by meeting the following requirements: Companies shall account for and report removals only if there is ongoing storage monitoring of the relevant carbon pool(s), as specified through a periodic monitoring plan, to demonstrate that the carbon remains stored or to detect losses of the stored carbon. Companies shall account for and report net carbon stock losses of previously reported removals in the year the losses occur, as either: Net CO2​ emissions, if the carbon pools are within the inventory boundary; or Reversals, if the carbon pools are no longer in the inventory boundary. If companies lose the ability to monitor carbon stocks associated with previously reported removals or if the monitoring plan is not renewed, companies shall assume previously reported removals are emitted and report net CO2​ emissions or reversals.,
summary: Mandates continuous monitoring for any carbon removal claims, with a requirement to report "reversals" if monitoring stops.
tags: carbon removals, permanence, monitoring plan, reversals

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: To achieve the "right to report" to account for scope 3 emission reductions or removals from a particular LMU, the reporting company should have documented consent from the landowner, land manager, or their proxy. This includes those who represent the owner or land managers, such as cooperatives or community-based organizations. When establishing a "right to report," it is the landowner's or land manager's decision about which GHG programs or systems the removals are accounted for and whom within a given GHG program or system can account for the removals. Where the "right to report" is provided by the landowner or operator to a customer of its products or supply chain initiatives, that "right to report" may cascade through the supply chain (i.e., it can be counted vertically across the different tiers from one shared value chain but not horizontally among the same tier from different value chains).,
summary: Describes the "right to report" as a formal mechanism for buyers to legally claim carbon removals from their suppliers.
tags: right to report, double counting, contract, ownership

doc_title: Land Sector and Removals Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall apply the same allocation method across accounting categories (i.e., emissions, removals, and other metrics) within a given spatial boundary. In most product life cycles, there is at least one common process that has multiple products as outputs, and for which it is not possible to collect data at the individual output level. In these situations, the total emissions, removals, and other metrics from the common process need to be partitioned among the multiple outputs. As a general principle, companies should select the allocation method that best reflects the causal relationship between the production of the outputs and the resulting emissions, removals, and other metrics, either because the physical properties of the product determine the emissions or the demand for a product determines the emissions. Companies should ensure that the same allocation methods are used for each process to avoid the over-counting or under-counting of total emissions.,,,
summary: Ensures suppliers use a single, consistent method for splitting emissions across multiple farm products to prevent data manipulation.
tags: allocation, co-products, consistency, metrics

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: If the organization has determined emissions to be a material topic, it is required to report gross Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 GHG emissions. When reporting gross Scope 1 and Scope 3 GHG emissions, organizations should include land use change emissions. Land use change refers to a change in the use or management of land by humans, which may lead to a change in land cover; for instance, when cropland is converted to grassland or when forests are converted to cropland. This includes natural ecosystem conversion. Organizations are also expected to disclose transition plans for climate change mitigation, GHG emissions reduction targets and progress, GHG removals in the value chain, and nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur oxides (SOx), and other significant air emissions.
summary: Outlines mandatory GHG reporting requirements including Scope 1-3 and the specific inclusion of land use change for agricultural suppliers.
tags: ghg emissions, scope 1 2 3, land use change, carbon targets

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: Organizations should describe policies or commitments to reduce or eliminate natural ecosystem conversion, including target and cut-off dates, for the organization’s own production, sourcing of terrestrial animal and fish feed, and products sourced by the organization for aggregation, processing, or trade. They should describe how the organization ensures that its suppliers comply with its natural ecosystem conversion policies or commitments, including through sourcing policies and contracts. A cut-off date is the date after which deforestation or conversion renders a given area or production unit non-compliant with no-deforestation or no-conversion commitments. Organizations are also encouraged to report their participation in multi-stakeholder, landscape, or sectoral initiatives intended to reduce or eliminate natural ecosystem conversion and describe the tools and systems used to monitor conversion in supply chains.
summary: Requires suppliers to use contracts and sourcing policies to enforce no-deforestation commitments across their own supply chains.
tags: deforestation-free, conversion-free, supplier contracts, monitoring

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: For products sourced by the organization, report by product the percentage of sourced volume determined to be deforestation- or conversion-free, and describe the assessment methods used. Assessment methods can include monitoring, certification, sourcing from low-risk jurisdictions with no or negligible recent conversion, or sourcing from verified suppliers. Additionally, report the percentage of sourced volume for which origins are not known to the point where it can be determined whether it is deforestation- or conversion-free, and describe actions taken to improve traceability. This includes reporting the size in hectares, location, and type of natural ecosystems converted since the cut-off date by suppliers or in sourcing locations. This ensures transparency regarding the environmental integrity of the agricultural raw materials being procured.
summary: Mandates disclosure of the percentage of deforestation-free sourced volumes and identification of untraceable supply chain portions.

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: Describe the pest management plan of the organization, including the rationale for the selection and application of pesticides and any other practices of pest control. This should include actions taken to prevent, mitigate and/or remediate negative impacts associated with the use of extremely and highly hazardous pesticides. Describe the actions, initiatives, or plans to switch to less hazardous pesticides and actions taken to optimize pest control practices. Furthermore, report the volume and intensity of pesticides used by toxicity hazard levels: extremely hazardous, highly hazardous, moderately hazardous, slightly hazardous, and unlikely to present an acute hazard. Organizations are also expected to describe the training provided to workers on pest management and the application of pesticides to ensure safety and minimize environmental toxicity.

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: Organizations are expected to report the percentage of production volume from sites certified to internationally recognized food safety standards and list these standards. Production volume refers to the total volume of products of the organization, including products sourced by the organization from suppliers. Certification programs, assurance schemes, or verification schemes provide a written assurance that a product is in conformity with certain safety requirements. Additionally, organizations should report the number of recalls issued for food safety reasons and the total volume of products recalled. This allows procurement teams to assess the reliability of a supplier's food safety management systems and their compliance with global safety benchmarks for consumer protection.
summary: Sets a benchmark for suppliers to disclose the percentage of their production volume covered by international food safety certifications.

doc_title: GRI 13: Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fishing Sectors 2022 V1.1
chunk_text: Describe policies regarding processing of animal products, animal transportation, handling, housing and confinement, and slaughter, by species. This includes describing the approach to animal health planning and involvement of veterinarians, as well as the approach to using anesthetic, antibiotic, anti-inflammatory, hormone, and growth-promotion treatments. Specifically, describe commitments for responsible and prudent use of antibiotics, such as avoiding prophylactic use, and describe how compliance with these commitments is evaluated. Organizations should also report the percentage of production volume from sites of the organization certified to third-party animal health and welfare standards. This information is critical for buyers to ensure that animal-derived products meet humane treatment expectations and public health standards regarding antimicrobial resistance.

chunk_text: Describe policies or commitments regarding recruitment of workers, including whether the organization has an ethical recruitment policy and whether these policies and commitments cover the approach to recruitment fees. chunk_text: Organizations should describe the approach to actions taken to determine and address situations where work undertaken within the supply chain does not take place within appropriate institutional and legal frameworks. chunk_text: For organizations in the fishing sector, describe policies, assurance schemes, and risk assessment processes related to illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of agricultural products sourced from Tier 1 supplier farms or facilities certified to a Global Food Safety Initiative (GFSI) recognised certification programme. The percentage shall be calculated as the cost of agricultural products sourced from Tier 1 suppliers certified to an applicable GFSI-recognised certification programme, divided by the total cost of agricultural products sourced from all Tier 1 suppliers. The scope of the disclosure excludes packaging materials or other goods and inputs that are not food or ingredients. The entity may disclose the relevant GFSI-recognised certification programme used to audit its suppliers. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of agricultural products, by cost, that it sourced that are certified to a third-party environmental or social standard. Agricultural products are defined as raw materials such as food, feed and biofuel ingredients sourced for use in the entity's operations. Environmental standards address impacts such as protection of primary forests, maintenance of water quality, and implementation of integrated pest management (IPM) or Organic System Plans. Social standards address impacts such as workforce compensation, training, and monitoring of health and safety risks associated with agrochemicals and child labour. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its supplier facilities' non-conformance rate with external social and environmental audit standards or internally developed supplier codes of conduct for major and minor non-conformances. A major non-conformance is defined as the highest severity requiring escalation, including the presence of underage child workers, forced labour, health and safety issues causing immediate danger to life, or environmental practices causing serious harm to the community. Major non-conformances include material breaches and systemic violations of code requirements or laws. The entity shall calculate non-conformance rates as the total number identified among its supplier facilities divided by the number of supplier facilities audited. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of agricultural products sourced from regions with High or Extremely High Baseline Water Stress. The percentage shall be calculated as the cost of agricultural products purchased from Tier 1 suppliers that withdraw and consume water in these regions divided by the total cost of agricultural products purchased from Tier 1 suppliers. The entity shall identify Tier 1 suppliers in these locations as classified by the World Resources Institute's (WRI) water risk atlas tool, Aqueduct. The scope includes products grown on a contract basis or sourced as a commodity. If the entity is unable to identify or collect data pertaining to all Tier 1 suppliers, the entity shall disclose the percentage of agricultural products for which the source region and water risks are unknown.

doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its gross global Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to the atmosphere of the seven GHGs covered under the Kyoto Protocol. Emissions shall be consolidated and disclosed in metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2​−e) and calculated in accordance with published 100-year time horizon global warming potential (GWP) values. Gross emissions are GHGs emitted before accounting for offsets or credits. Scope 1 emissions shall be calculated according to the methodology contained in The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard. Data shall be consolidated according to the approach with which the entity consolidates its financial reporting data, generally aligned with the 'financial control' approach. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its total recordable incident rate (TRIR), fatality rate, and near miss frequency rate (NMFR) for direct employees and contract employees. Direct employees are defined as individuals on the entity's payroll. Contract employees are defined as individuals who are not on the entity's payroll but whom the entity supervises or manages, including independent contractors and those employed by third parties such as temp agencies and labour brokers. All disclosed rates shall be calculated as: (statistic count x 200,000) / total number of hours worked. The scope of the disclosure includes all employees regardless of location or type of employment. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategy to manage environmental and social risks that arise from its contract growing and commodity sourcing practices. Environmental risks include extreme weather events, water stress, and degradation of the environment. Social risks include labour rights, community rights and harmful child labour practices. Relevant strategies include the diversification of suppliers, supplier training programmes on environmental best management practices—including agricultural management practice systems (MPS) for fertiliser use and integrated pest management (IPM)—and efforts to address deforestation. For social risks, strategies include training on agrochemical application, engagement on issues relating to human rights and pesticide exposure, and maintenance of a supply chain code of conduct. doc_title: Agricultural Products Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall identify any principal crops that are a priority to its business and describe the risks or opportunities presented by climate change scenarios. Principal crops are those accounting for 10% or more of consolidated revenue. The scope includes crops cultivated directly, grown on a contract basis, or sourced as a commodity. Risks may include availability of water, shifts in crop regions, pest migration and extreme weather events. The entity shall discuss the scenarios used, the timeline over which risks manifest, and efforts to assess and monitor impacts. Alleviation strategies may include crop insurance, hedging, and supply chain diversification. Adaptation strategies may include improving ecosystem management, development of tolerant crop varieties and optimising timing of planting and harvesting.

chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategy to manage the use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs), including a discussion of jurisdictions that restrict the importation of GMOs, the risks associated with required labelling, changes in consumer preferences, and opportunities associated with GMO use. The entity shall disclose a list of jurisdictions that restrict, ban or suspend imports of one or more of the entity's products because of regulations on GMOs. doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total amount of fuel consumed by its fleet vehicles as an aggregate figure, in gigajoules (GJ). The calculation methodology for fuel consumed shall be based on actual fuel consumed as opposed to design parameters. Acceptable calculation methodologies for fuel consumed may include methodologies based on: adding fuel purchases made during the reporting period to beginning inventory at the start of the reporting period, less any fuel inventory at the end of the reporting period; tracking fuel consumed by vehicles; and tracking fuel expenses. The entity shall also disclose the percentage of the total amount of fuel consumed by its fleet vehicles that is renewable fuel. Renewable fuel generally is defined as fuel that meets all the following requirements: produced from renewable biomass; used to replace or reduce the quantity of fossil fuel present in a transportation fuel, heating oil or jet fuel; and achieved net greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction on a life cycle basis. The scope of disclosure includes fuel consumed by vehicles owned or operated by the entity.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its gross global Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to the atmosphere of the seven GHGs covered under the Kyoto Protocol—carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3)—that originated from the use of refrigerants. Emissions of all GHGs shall be consolidated and disclosed in metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-e) and calculated in accordance with published 100-year time horizon global warming potential (GWP) values. Scope 1 emissions are defined and shall be calculated according to the methodology contained in The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard. The scope of emissions includes all direct emissions of GHGs resulting from the entity's use of commercial stationary and mobile refrigerants in retail locations, distribution centres and its transportation fleet. doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total weight of food waste and unsaleable food generated, in metric tonnes. Food waste is defined as food and inedible parts for which the entity has no further use that are removed from the food supply chain. Unsaleable food is defined as food safe for human consumption, but that is unavailable for sale because of issues related to quality, over-production or labelling. The entity shall describe the quantification methods used to calculate the amount of food waste and inedible parts, including the measurement or approximation method used (e.g., direct weighting, counting, assessing volume) and the calculation used (e.g., mass balance, modelling or proxy data). The entity shall also disclose the percentage of food waste or unsaleable food, by weight, that was diverted or rescued. Food waste is considered diverted if it has been used as feed for animals, converted for use in bio-based industrial products, broken down via bacteria (codigested or fermented), composted, or tilled into the soil. Unsaleable food is considered rescued if it has been donated to social service agencies or charitable organisations.
