doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its approach to identifying information system vulnerabilities that may pose a data security risk. Vulnerability is defined as a weakness in an information system, implementation, system security procedure or internal control that could be exploited. Data security risk is defined as the risk of any circumstance or event with the potential to affect organisational operations adversely through an information system via unauthorised access, destruction, disclosure, modification of information or denial of service. The entity shall describe its approach to managing identified data security risks and vulnerabilities, which may include operational procedures, management processes, structure of products, selection of business partners, employee training and use of technology. The entity may describe the degree to which its approach aligns with an external standard or framework for managing data security, such as the ISO/IEC 27000 series or the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total number of food-safety-related recalls it issued during the reporting period, including voluntary and involuntary recalls. A food-safety-related recall is defined as the removal of a marketed product that occurs if a food may reasonably be believed to cause consumers to become ill. The entity shall disclose the total number of units of food products subject to food-safety-related recalls and the percentage of those units that were private-label products. A private-label product is defined as a store-brand product packaged for sale with a retailer's brand name, whether manufactured by the retailer or by another manufacturer. The entity shall provide a discussion of notable recalls, such as those that affected a significant number of products or those related to potential or actual serious illnesses or fatalities. For such recalls, the entity may provide a description and cause of the recall issue, the total quantity of food products recalled, cost to remedy the issue, whether the recall was voluntary or involuntary, corrective actions, and any other significant outcomes.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its revenue from products sold during the reporting period labelled as (1) containing genetically modified organisms (GMOs), and separately, (2) not containing GMOs (non-GMOs). GMOs are defined as organisms, except for human beings, in which genetic material has been altered in a way that does not occur naturally by mating or natural recombination. For the purposes of this disclosure, products that are third-party certified to standards for which non-GMO is inherent to the certification shall be considered to be labelled 'non-GMO'. The entity may disclose the revenue from its products labelled as containing GMOs and non-GMOs in jurisdictions subject to GMO labelling regulation. Consumers may seek additional information about product ingredients, such as the presence of GMO content. This issue can affect competition among entities in the industry, since entities may be subject to litigation or criticism resulting from making misleading statements or failing to adapt to consumer demand for increased labelling transparency.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the total amount of monetary losses incurred during the reporting period resulting from legal proceedings associated with (1) labour law violations and (2) employment discrimination. Labour violation is defined as violations which may include those relating to wages, work hours, overtime, and meal and rest breaks. Employment discrimination is defined as discrimination based on age, disability, genetic information, national origin, pregnancy, race/colour, religion or gender. The legal proceedings shall include any adjudicative proceeding involving the entity, whether before a court, a regulator, an arbitrator, or otherwise. The losses shall include all monetary liabilities to the opposing party or to others (whether as the result of settlement, verdict after trial or otherwise), including fines and other monetary liabilities incurred during the reporting period as a result of civil actions, regulatory proceedings and criminal actions. The entity shall briefly describe the nature and context of all monetary losses resulting from legal proceedings and describe any corrective actions implemented in response, such as specific changes in operations, management, or training.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its revenue from products third-party certified to an environmental or social sustainability standard. Environmental standards are defined as standards that address environmental impacts related to the production of agricultural products such as protection of primary forests, maintenance of surface water and groundwater quality, and implementation of integrated pest management (IPM) solutions or an Organic System Plan. Social standards are defined as standards that address social impacts related to the production of agricultural products such as compensation of the workforce, training and continual monitoring of health and safety risks associated with applications of agrochemicals, and child-labour practices. Examples of certifications to third-party environmental and social standards may include: Bonsucro; Fairtrade International; Fair Trade USA; Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO); Roundtable on Responsible Soy (RTRS); Rainforest Alliance; SA8000; U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Organic; and UTZ Certified. doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategic approach to managing its environmental and social risks present within its food products supply chain, specifically including animal welfare standards applicable to its supply chain. Animal welfare standards are defined as policies for beef, pork, poultry or dairy production conditions, including animal treatment and handling; housing and transportation conditions; and slaughter facilities and procedures. The entity shall disclose the percentage of revenue from eggs sold that originated from a cage-free environment. Eggs that originated from a cage-free environment are defined as those produced by hens housed in a space that allows for unrestricted access to food and water and provides freedom to roam within the space. Additionally, the entity shall disclose the percentage of revenue from pork produced without the use of gestation crates. A gestation crate is defined as an enclosure for housing an individual breeding sow that is restrictive enough to prevent dynamic movements, such as turning around. This information helps manage reputational risks and potentially captures new market opportunities associated with humane treatment expectations.

doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategies to reduce the environmental impact of packaging, such as optimising packaging weight and volume for a given application, or using alternative materials, including those that are renewable, recycled, recyclable or compostable. Relevant disclosures may include design innovations, such as strategies to optimise the amount of material used; packaging weight, shape and size; product-to-package ratio; cube utilisation and void fill. The entity may discuss its strategies as they relate to primary, secondary and tertiary packaging of its private-label products as well as the packaging of products from its vendors. Primary packaging comes into direct contact with the product, while secondary and tertiary packaging are used for grouping and transport. The entity may also discuss its use of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) analysis in the context of its approach to environmental impact reduction and maximisation of product efficiency, including weight reduction and transportation efficiency. doc_title: Food Retailers & Distributors Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategic approach to managing environmental and social risks present within, or which may arise out of, its food and food products supply chain. Environmental and social risks may include impacts on crop and livestock production because of climate change (e.g., water stress), animal feed price increases, fuel economy regulations, labour rights, and commercial catch limits. Relevant strategies to discuss may include supplier screening, diversification of suppliers, supplier training programmes on best environmental management practices, supplier engagement on labour and human rights issues, and maintenance of a supply chain code of conduct, supply chain audits and certifications. The entity shall identify which products or product lines present risks to its operations, the risks represented and the strategies the entity uses to mitigate such risks. Effective management of these product supply risks improves supply chain resiliency and mitigates reputational risks. doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall collect data for all processes included in the inventory boundary. Companies shall collect primary data for all processes under their ownership or control. Primary data can be process activity data (physical measures of a process that results in GHG emissions or removals), direct emissions data (determined through direct monitoring, stoichiometry, mass balance, or similar methods) from a specific site, or data that is averaged across all sites that contain the specific process. Primary data can be measured or modeled, as long as the result is specific to the process in the product’s life cycle. It is important to note that using the reference flow of the studied product (e.g., mass of finished product) as process activity data is not considered primary data. Allocated data are considered primary data as long as the data meets the other primary data requirements.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: For significant processes, companies shall report a descriptive statement on the data sources, the data quality, and any efforts taken to improve data quality. Companies need to determine which processes are significant in order to report the data sources, quality concerns, and quality improvement efforts. For example, a process that contributes a substantial amount of GHG emissions relative to the total life cycle emissions is significant. Reporting includes a qualitative description of uncertainty sources and methodological choices. Methodological choices include: use and end-of-life profile; allocation methods, including allocation due to recycling; source of global warming potential (GWP) values used; and calculation models. This allows stakeholders to evaluate the reliability of data and the rigor of the inventory process for those activities that dominate the carbon footprint.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall account for carbon dioxide (CO2​), methane (CH4​), nitrous oxide (N2​O), sulfur hexafluoride (SF6​), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) emissions to, and removals from, the atmosphere. Additional GHGs included in the inventory shall be listed in the inventory report. Companies shall account for these six gases in their product GHG inventory if they are emitted during the product’s life cycle. Companies should account for any other GHGs whose 100-year GWP values have been identified by the IPCC if they are emitted during the product’s life cycle. Any additional GHGs that are accounted for shall be listed in the inventory report to improve transparency. Removals from the atmosphere typically occur when CO2​ is absorbed by biogenic sources (i.e. plants) and converted to energy during photosynthesis. Companies shall also account for all removals of CO2​ from the atmosphere if they are removed during the product’s life cycle.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: The product GHG inventory shall be assured by a first or third party. Companies shall choose assurance providers that are independent of, and have no conflicts of interest with, the product GHG inventory process. Assurers are defined as person(s) providing assurance over the product inventory and shall be independent of any involvement in the determination of the product inventory or development of any declaration. Assurers shall have no conflicts of interests, such that they can exercise objective and impartial judgment. Companies shall report the assurance statement in the inventory report. The statement shall include: whether the assurance was performed by a first or third party; the level of assurance achieved (limited or reasonable) including assurance opinion or the critical review findings; a summary of the assurance process; and the relevant competencies of the assurance providers.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: For all final products, companies shall define the unit of analysis as a functional unit. Final products are goods and services that are ultimately consumed by the end user rather than used in the production of another good or service. The functional unit is defined as the performance characteristics and services delivered by the product being studied. A defined functional unit typically includes the function (service) a product fulfills, the duration or service life (amount of time needed to fulfill the function), and the expected quality level. For intermediate products where the eventual function is unknown, companies shall define the unit of analysis as the reference flow. Intermediate products are goods that are used as inputs in the production of other goods and services. A well-defined unit of analysis is important to ensure inventory results are interpreted and used correctly and allows for tracking efficiency improvements over time.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall avoid allocation wherever possible by using process subdivision, redefining the functional unit, or using system expansion. If allocation is unavoidable, companies shall allocate emissions and removals based on the underlying physical relationships between the studied product and co-product(s). When physical relationships alone cannot be established or used as the basis for allocation, companies shall select either economic allocation or another allocation method that reflects other relationships between the studied product and co-product(s). Companies shall apply the same allocation methods to similar inputs and outputs within the product's life cycle. Companies shall disclose and justify the methods used to avoid allocation or perform allocation due to co-products or recycling. For allocation due to recycling, companies shall use either the closed loop approximation method or the recycled content method as defined by this standard.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: For allocation due to recycling, companies shall use either the closed loop approximation method or the recycled content method. The closed loop approximation method accounts for the impact that end-of-life recycling has on the net virgin acquisition of a material. Its name derives from the assumption that the material being recycled is used to displace virgin material input with the same inherent properties. The recycled content method allocates the recycling process emissions and removals to the life cycle that uses the recycled material. If neither method is appropriate, companies may use another method if the method conforms to the allocation requirements, accounts for all emissions and removals due to recycling, and applies an allocation factor consistently between inputs and outputs. When using the closed loop approximation method, companies shall report displaced emissions and removals separately from the studied product's end-of-life stage inventory.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall report the method used to calculate land-use change impacts, when applicable. Land-use impacts are attributable to a product if the following are true: the carbon stock change is the direct result of extraction or production of biogenic material to create a product; the carbon stock change was caused by human intervention with the intent of creating a product; and the carbon stock change occurred within the assessment period of 20 years or a single harvest period, whichever timeframe is longer. Land-use change impacts include biogenic CO2​ emissions and removals due to carbon stock change occurring as a result of land conversion within or between land use categories and emissions resulting from the preparation of converted land, such as biomass burning or liming. When land-use change impacts are attributable, companies shall include these in the boundary and disclose the calculation method in the inventory report.

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies can better model potential future costs of regulations by using a product inventory to evaluate a product's life cycle GHG risks. Business goals served by a product GHG inventory include: partnering with suppliers to achieve GHG reductions; assessing supplier performance for GHG aspects of green procurement efforts; and reducing GHG emissions and energy use, costs, and risks in the supply chain and avoiding future costs related to energy and emissions. Product inventories provide detailed information on the relative size and scale of emission sources within life cycle stages and across the entire product system. This information may be used to identify the largest emission sources—or "hot spots"—in the life cycle and focus efforts on the most cost-effective emissions reduction activities. Reporting on these types of efforts and the progress of a company’s engagement with its suppliers can be useful information for stakeholders.
summary: Identifies how enterprise buyers use product inventories as a benchmark for green procurement and supplier evaluation.,

doc_title: Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard
chunk_text: Companies shall quantify and report the total inventory results in CO2​e per unit of analysis. Total results shall include all emissions and removals from biogenic sources, non-biogenic sources, and land-use change impacts. Companies shall not include weighting factors for delayed emissions, offsets, and avoided emissions when quantifying inventory results. Separately, companies shall quantify and report: percentage of total inventory results by life cycle stage; biogenic and non-biogenic emissions and removals separately; land-use change impacts separately; and cradle-to-gate and gate-to-gate inventory results separately (or a clear statement that confidentiality is a limitation). Companies shall report the amount of carbon contained in the product or its components that is not released to the atmosphere during waste treatment, if applicable. For cradle-to-gate inventories, companies shall report the amount of carbon contained in the intermediate product.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total amount of energy it consumed as an aggregate figure, in gigajoules (GJ). The scope of energy consumption includes energy from all sources, including energy purchased from external sources and energy produced by the entity itself (self-generated). For example, direct fuel usage, purchased electricity, and heating, cooling and steam energy are all included within the scope of energy consumption. The scope of energy consumption includes only energy directly consumed by the entity during the reporting period. In calculating energy consumption from fuels and biofuels, the entity shall use higher heating values (HHV), also known as gross calorific values (GCV), which are measured directly or taken from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). The entity shall apply conversion factors consistently for all data reported under this disclosure, such as the use of HHVs for fuel usage and conversion of kilowatt hours (kWh) to GJ.
summary: Establishes the requirement for suppliers to report total energy consumption using standardized units (GJ) and specific heating value calculations.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: Renewable energy is defined as energy from sources that are replenished at a rate greater than or equal to their rate of depletion, such as geothermal, wind, solar, hydro and biomass. The scope of renewable energy includes renewable fuel the entity consumed, renewable energy the entity directly produced and renewable energy the entity purchased, if purchased through a renewable power purchase agreement (PPA) that explicitly includes renewable energy certificates (RECs) or Guarantees of Origin (GOs). For any renewable electricity generated on-site, any RECs and GOs shall be retained (not sold) and retired or cancelled on behalf of the entity for the entity to claim them as renewable energy. For renewable PPAs and green power products, the agreement shall explicitly include and convey that RECs and GOs be retained or replaced and retired or cancelled on behalf of the entity for the entity to claim them as renewable energy.
summary: Defines the strict criteria for what a supplier can claim as "renewable energy," emphasizing the necessity of retiring certificates.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall analyse all its operations for water risks and identify activities that withdraw and consume water in locations with High (40–80%) or Extremely High (>80%) Baseline Water Stress as classified by the World Resources Institute’s (WRI) Water Risk Atlas tool, Aqueduct. The entity shall disclose the amount of water, in thousands of cubic metres, withdrawn from all sources and the amount consumed in its operations. Water consumption is defined as water that evaporates during withdrawal, use and discharge; water that is directly or indirectly incorporated into the entity's product or service; and water that does not otherwise return to the same catchment area from which it was withdrawn. The entity shall disclose water withdrawn in locations with High or Extremely High Baseline Water Stress as a percentage of the total water withdrawn and consumed.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe its approach to identifying information system vulnerabilities that may pose a data security risk. Vulnerability is defined as a weakness in an information system, implementation, system security procedure or internal control that could be exploited. Data security risk is defined as the risk of any circumstance or event with the potential to affect organisational operations, assets, individuals, or other organisations through an information system via unauthorised access, destruction, disclosure, modification of information or denial of service. The entity shall describe its approach to managing identified data security risks and vulnerabilities which may include operational procedures, management processes, structure of products, selection of business partners, employee training and use of technology. The entity may describe the degree to which its approach aligns with an external standard or framework, such as the ISO/IEC 27000-series or the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity.
summary: Requires suppliers to detail their cybersecurity risk management and identifies industry-standard frameworks (ISO/NIST) used for evaluation.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total number of data breaches identified during the reporting period and (2) the percentage of data breaches that were personal data breaches. A data breach is defined as an unauthorised occurrence on, or conducted through, an entity's information systems that jeopardises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of an entity's information systems or any information contained therein. A personal data breach is defined as a data breach resulting in the accidental or unauthorised destruction, loss, alteration, disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed. The entity shall describe any corrective actions taken in response to data breaches, such as changes in operations, management, processes, products, business partners, training or technology. All disclosure shall be sufficient such that it is specific to the risks the entity faces, but disclosure itself would not compromise the entity's ability to maintain data privacy and security.
summary: Mandates reporting of the frequency and nature of data breaches, specifically requiring evidence of corrective actions taken in response.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the percentage of gender and diversity group representation among its employees for (a) executive management, (b) non-executive management, (c) technical employees and (d) all other employees. Executive management is defined as chief executives and senior officials who formulate and review policies. Technical employees are defined as employees who perform highly skilled work generally categorised in computing, mathematical, architectural and engineering occupations. Diversity is defined as the presence of people from populations who have been underrepresented in a particular field or are otherwise historically marginalised. Diversity groups may be defined by dimensions such as race, ethnicity, disability status, region of origin, migrant status, indigenous background, age, socioeconomic background, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity. The entity shall describe its policies and programmes for fostering equitable employee representation, such as transparency of hiring, promotion and wage practices, and ensuring equal employment opportunities.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the complete tank-to-wheels greenhouse gas (GHG) footprint, in metric tonnes of CO2​−e, associated with outbound shipment of the entity's products. Tank-to-wheels emissions relate to vehicle processes and exclude upstream emissions associated with primary energy production. The entity shall calculate its disclosure according to EN 16258:2012 - Methodology for calculation and declaration of energy consumption and GHG emissions of transport services. The scope of disclosure includes emissions from all freight transportation and logistics activities associated with the outbound shipment of the entity's products, including those from contract carriers and outsourced freight forwarding services and logistics providers (Scope 3) as well as those from the entity's own assets (Scope 1). The scope includes emissions from all modes of transportation, such as road freight, air freight, barge transport, marine transport, and rail transport.

doc_title: E-commerce Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall discuss its strategies to reduce the environmental impact of fulfilment and product delivery, including impacts associated with packaging materials and product transportation. Relevant strategies include: logistics selection and mode selection for route efficiency; packaging choices such as using recycled or renewable material (e.g., bio-based plastic), optimising the amount of packaging materials (source reduction), use of refillable or reusable packaging, and design for efficient shipping; and fuel and vehicle choices for fleets owned or operated by the entity, such as decisions to use renewable and low-emission fuels and low-emission vehicles. Other relevant strategies include efforts to reduce idling of vehicles, innovations to improve the efficiency of 'last-mile' delivery and strategies to optimise delivery times to reduce traffic congestion. These actions permit entities to reduce shipping costs through fuel reduction and more efficient routing.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: All entities in Kenya are permitted to apply the ISSB Standards for annual financial reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2024. However, mandatory application is phased based on the entity type according to the Roadmap for Adoption of IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards in Kenya. Public interest entities, which include listed entities, are mandated to apply the ISSB Standards for annual financial reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2027. Non-public interest entities, categorized as large entities, are mandated to apply the ISSB Standards for annual financial reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2028. Finally, small- to medium-sized entities are mandated to apply the ISSB Standards for annual financial reporting periods commencing on or after 1 January 2029. This roadmap provides a clear regulatory timeline for when different classes of suppliers must begin formal sustainability reporting.
summary: Mandatory implementation timeline for ISSB standards in Kenya, phased by entity size from 2027 to 2029.
tags: issb, ifrs s1, ifrs s2, compliance timeline

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: The legal and regulatory framework for sustainability-related disclosures in Kenya adopts IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information and IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures. Under these requirements, an entity is required to disclose material information about the sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect its cash flows, its access to finance or the cost of capital over the short, medium or long term. These sustainability-related financial disclosures are required to be published at the same time as the related financial statements and must be included as part of general purpose financial reports. This requirement ensures that sustainability information is provided with the same timing and placement as traditional financial data, enabling investors, lenders, and enterprise buyers to evaluate the entity's long-term financial resilience and risk exposure.
source_section_or_page: Extent of application of ISSB Standards, p. 1
summary: Requirement for entities to disclose material sustainability risks and opportunities alongside their financial statements.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: The Roadmap for Adoption of IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards in Kenya provides an ‘assurance roadmap’ setting out a phased approach that begins with voluntary limited assurance and concludes with mandatory reasonable assurance. For public interest entities, fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025 allow for voluntary limited assurance. Mandatory limited assurance begins on 1 January 2028, followed by mandatory reasonable assurance on 1 January 2029. Notably, limited assurance will continue to apply to disclosures about Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions until 1 January 2030, at which point mandatory reasonable assurance will be required for all disclosures. This phased implementation of assurance requirements signals to procurement professionals the increasing level of data reliability they can expect from Kenyan suppliers' sustainability reports over the coming years.
summary: Phased roadmap for voluntary and mandatory assurance of sustainability disclosures, including specific timelines for Scope 3.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: Mandatory sustainability disclosure requirements in Kenya apply to entities considered to be ‘public interest entities’. This includes any publicly traded entity, an entity one of whose main functions is to take deposits from the public, or an entity one of whose main functions is to provide insurance to the public. It also includes entities specified as such by law, regulation or professional standards reflecting significant public interest in the financial condition of such an entity due to the potential impact of their financial well-being on stakeholders. Furthermore, foreign publicly accountable entities are required to report in accordance with the same framework as domestic publicly accountable entities. Enterprise buyers should note that any large-scale Kenyan supplier falling into these categories will be subject to the earliest mandatory reporting requirements starting in 2027.
summary: Definition of public interest entities subject to mandatory ISSB reporting, including financial institutions and foreign entities.
tags: public interest entities, financial institutions, foreign entities, listed companies

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: In Kenya, the jurisdiction’s legal or regulatory framework requires entities to make an explicit and unreserved statement of compliance with IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards as issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). ‘Dual reporting’ is not allowed, meaning entities may not assert compliance both with ISSB Standards and another set of standards. However, listed entities are permitted to provide additional disclosures, such as applying GRI Standards for sustainability-related risks and opportunities not addressed by the ISSB Standards. In such cases, the entity is required to ensure that information required by ISSB Standards is not obscured and that the additional disclosures are clearly identified. This ensures a consistent baseline of financial sustainability information while allowing suppliers to address broader stakeholder interests through supplementary frameworks without compromising the core reporting standard.
summary: Prohibition of dual reporting and requirements for using supplementary frameworks like GRI alongside ISSB.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Kenya
chunk_text: Several jurisdictional authorities in Kenya are responsible for the oversight and implementation of sustainability reporting. The Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya (ICPAK) is the local professional accountancy organisation and standard-setting body with a legislative mandate to issue financial reporting standards. The Capital Markets Authority (CMA) has primary responsibility for supervising and monitoring market intermediaries and issues regulations for capital market entities. The Nairobi Securities Exchange PLC provides the platform for listing and issues rules requiring entities to produce financial statements in accordance with the framework issued by ICPAK. Additionally, the Central Bank of Kenya provides the legal and regulatory framework and issues prudential guidelines for financial institutions. For procurement-focused assessments, these authorities represent the regulatory infrastructure that ensures the validity and enforcement of supplier sustainability disclosures in the Kenyan market.
summary: Overview of the regulatory bodies in Kenya responsible for enforcing and monitoring sustainability disclosure standards.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: The GRI Standards represent a global practice to report sustainability management and performance, which facilitates the comparability and quality of the information reported. The Standards are structured in a modular way, divided according to universal and thematic indicators (economic, social and environmental), and are interrelated. By using the GRI Standards, a complete and balanced image is projected of the priority issues for an organization and the related impacts, as well as the management of these impacts. Thanks to this, the GRI Standards have become the common language used by companies in sharing their sustainability impacts in a transparent manner. For example, 73% of the world’s largest 250 companies (the G250) use the GRI Standards and 168 policies in 63 countries and regions reference or require the GRI Standards for their regulations. For Peruvian MSMEs, more than 1,200 have been trained on the GRI Standards. The sustainability report is a management and communication tool that allows organizations to manage their impacts, identify strengths and points for improvement, and increase credibility within and outside the organization.
summary: Overview of the GRI Standards as a global benchmark for transparent sustainability reporting and impact management.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: GRI 205: Anti-corruption 2016 manages and communicates issues related to anti-corruption, including operations assessed for risks related to corruption, training about anti-corruption policies, and confirmed incidents of corruption. Identifying and managing conflicts of interest of employees as well as stakeholders in relation to organization’s activities, services or products is one of the remits of the Standard. MSMEs manage anti-corruption by reviewing their processes and activities and identifying production risks; creating and publishing their anti-corruption policies; and creating a notification channel around incidents and/or alleged corruption cases in the company. They also train their personnel on how to reduce corruption risks and communicate the company’s anti-corruption policy with their employees and strategic partners – like their suppliers. MSMEs evaluate their anti-corruption management performance by communicating their anti-corruption policy and the reported incidents in the calendar year. They also measure the number of trained employees or the hours of anti-corruption training invested. These improvements allow companies to have a work plan that considers economic, social, and environmental aspects.
summary: Specific operational practices for anti-corruption management, including risk assessment, policy creation, and training for employees and suppliers.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Materials Standard 301 manages and communicates the impacts of materials used by an organization. This Standard allows the organization to include the total calculation of materials, defined as: raw materials necessary for the production process; semi-manufactured articles or pieces that are part of the final product; and packaging materials, including paper, cardboard, and plastics. Reporting on the materials used in production allows the organization to objectively measure the quantity of materials, the type (renewable or non-renewable), which ones have the potential to be recycled or recovered and, finally, measure their negative or positive impact on the environment. MSMEs manage materials by identifying the potential for reuse or recycling of each of these materials and identifying the types of materials and their quantity in their packing or packaging. They evaluate their performance by reporting the increase or decrease in kilograms or tons of each material, classifying them by type, uses in the production process and / or potential for reuse or recycling. Evaluation of the design of processes and / or products to reduce waste is a key management strategy.
summary: Framework for tracking and reporting material consumption, including raw materials and packaging, with a focus on recyclability.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Standard 403 on Health and Safety at Work is designed to inform stakeholders about the management of the health and safety of workers. Occupational health and safety management systems are an effective method to continuously manage and eliminate hazards and minimize risks. MSMEs manage the health and safety of workers by ensuring compliance with the standards set by law; evaluating the risks of all processes based on potential impacts to health and safety of workers; and implementing health and safety systems at work. They also carry out training or education programs for workers and obtain additional certifications in health and safety at work. Performance is evaluated by indicators that show a decrease or increase in incidents, accidents and fatalities. For example, some SMEs have created the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) supervisor role and implemented an incident and accident registration system, as well as a record of the state of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). If employees are able to see that the company is concerned for their safety, then they will feel more motivated and committed to their work.
summary: Mandatory components of an Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) system, including hazard identification, supervisor roles, and PPE tracking.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: The 404 Training and Education Standard informs stakeholders about the impacts related to training of workers, covering average hours of training per year per employee and programs for upgrading employee skills. Measuring the training and skill level of their employees allows organizations to plan what skills and knowledge are required for them to obtain better results within the company. Having more qualified workers enhances the organization’s human capital and contributes to their satisfaction and motivation, which is directly related to their performance. MSMEs manage the Training and Education of their workers by identifying new training topics relevant to workers and their performance and scheduling structured training and education programs throughout the year. They use indicators to measure performance such as the number of hours provided per worker on external and internal training and the number of programs or workshops provided at every level of the organization. By concentrating on training staff, both the productivity of the company and the work environment improve. When needs of employees and company obligations are not compatible, companies evaluate financial options for education.
summary: Benchmark for measuring and managing employee training hours and skill development programs to improve productivity.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Standard 405, Diversity and Equal Opportunity, manages diversity within an organization, including the diversity of governance bodies and employees and the ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men. The disclosures provide quantitative data on diversity and can be used to make comparisons with industry or regional standards. MSMEs manage diversity by developing an equal opportunities policy; reviewing the minimum legal requirements regarding diversity; and reviewing their selection or recruitment processes to avoid bias. They also review their salary policies to verify that there are no gender disparities and carry out awareness programs for workers on diversity and equal opportunities. Evaluation indicators include the number of workers per gender, the number of processes reviewed to avoid gender bias, and the number of training sessions on equal opportunities and diversity. Some companies have formed gender committees to promote equal opportunities and prevent gender violence at work. Involving women in institutional decision-making is an opportunity to improve reputation amongst partners. Managing diversity broadens organizational culture and brings satisfying results.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Energy Standard 302 manages and communicates the impacts related to organization’s energy consumption management. When reporting about its energy consumption, an organization can show to its stakeholders if it complies with the minimum requirements set by Peruvian law in relation to that sector’s energy consumption. The greatest benefit that companies identify when reporting their energy consumption is that it brings out the most significant savings opportunities, even for non-manufacturing companies. MSMEs manage energy consumption by measuring their consumption on a regular basis; identifying opportunities to reduce consumption in plants and offices; and informing staff about environmental impacts. They evaluate their performance by monitoring and measuring energy consumption on a monthly basis, often tracking the economic savings generated after improvements. For example, some SMEs monitor monthly consumption through a format that compares electricity and water bills to see if service costs are decreasing. Others invest in machinery to reduce production times and energy costs, or change workshop and office lights to LED lights. Designing workshop spaces to use natural light for as long as possible is also recommended.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Standard 413 for Local Communities informs stakeholders about the impacts, expectations and interests of the organizations’ nearby communities. Two key elements in managing impacts on local communities are assessment and planning, aimed to better understand current and potential impacts. Assessment and planning should also involve the local communities to understand their expectations and needs. Organizations are expected to anticipate and avoid negative impacts on local communities. MSMEs manage their relationship with the community through programs designed for the community to actively participate in activities of positive impact for the locality and capacity reinforcement programs on topics of interest to the community and the company. Indicators include satisfaction surveys within the communities or the number of programs implemented. Companies should be aware that they are part of society and doing business is not enough. We have the responsibility to share a territory and society, being attentive to community needs and prompting clients to support social and environmental programs. Cooperation between companies and communities can improve environmental protection practices and promote sustainable tourism.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: Standard 306 manages and informs stakeholders about the impacts associated with an organization’s waste management, focusing significantly on circular economy. This Standard is based on the premise that an organization can generate waste throughout its value chain, not only on the production stage. It requires organizations to share total weight metrics of all residues and show the calculation methodologies. MSMEs manage their waste by measuring the amount of waste produced throughout their value chain; identifying opportunities to reuse waste; raising awareness among staff on reuse of materials; and using waste as raw materials for new products (circular economy principle). Performance is evaluated by measuring the number of hours of awareness raising on recycling; the amount of waste reduced; the number of partnerships developed with other organizations to manage waste; and additional income generated by the sale of products created from reused waste. The consequences of climate change lead us to believe that the economy of the future must be circular and have a low carbon footprint. We must continue to work efficiently, addressing the end of life of our products.

doc_title: Best practices in sustainability by Peruvian MSMEs
chunk_text: The Competitive Business Program helps large companies strengthen sustainability and traceability in their supply chains, reducing risks and strengthening reputation by assuming responsibility for impacts. Some SMEs identify that their main manufacturing suppliers lack knowledge of basic business topics such as cost structure, logistics and fair trade. To ensure the quality of the entire supply chain, companies commit to promoting the development of their suppliers through workshops. These workshops provide appraisal skills required to improve negotiation capabilities and increase income. Increased loyalty from suppliers ensures the quality of products over time. It is recommended to visit suppliers frequently to identify further training opportunities that lead to the continuous improvement of their services. Companies also share knowledge with their clients to help them better understand the market. For example, offering smaller local hardware stores special discounts regardless of purchase volume and providing training on product types helps them improve their profit margins and educate their own clients. By sharing knowledge, everyone in the value chain grows and strengthens the corporate trust.

chunk_text: BRSR Lite targets smaller companies, including unlisted entities, aiming to make sustainability reporting more accessible. It offers a simplified and condensed reporting format compared to the Comprehensive version. BRSR Lite focuses on key ESG areas relevant to the company’s size and industry, such as identifying material ESG aspects, responsible sourcing practices within the supply chain, and stakeholder engagement. It encourages smaller companies to initiate ESG reporting without overwhelming demands by allowing qualitative narratives and less comprehensive data for disclosures. This flexible approach accommodates smaller companies' resources while establishing a baseline for ESG performance.

doc_title: Background Material on Sustainability and Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)
chunk_text: Sustainable sourcing is the integration of social, ethical and environmental performance factors into the process of selecting suppliers. It includes purchasing sustainably preferable products and services, such as products made from recycled or remanufactured materials, as well as green purchasing guidelines. Entities are required to disclose the proportion of their inputs (by quantity or value) sourced from suppliers covered by the company’s sustainable sourcing programs. They should also identify suppliers certified to be compliant with social and environmental standards such as SA 8000, ISO 14001, OHSAS 18001, or relevant labels like Rainforest Alliance and RSPO. These practices help manage risks related to brand protection and supply chain disruptions.

doc_title: Background Material on Sustainability and Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)
chunk_text: The listed entity must provide a list of its value chain partners, including suppliers, contractors, and joint venture partners. It is required to assess the sustainability risks associated with these partners, considering environmental, social, and governance factors like labor practices and human rights. The entity must describe the measures it is taking to mitigate these sustainability risks. This may include working with partners to improve their performance, providing training and support, or conducting regular audits. The scope of the assessment should be based on the materiality of the sustainability risks associated with the value chain partners.

chunk_text: Scope 3 emissions are indirect GHG emissions that occur outside of the organization, including both upstream and downstream activities. Upstream categories can include purchased goods and services, capital goods, upstream transportation and distribution, and business travel. Entities are encouraged to provide details of total Scope 3 emissions and their intensity in metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent per rupee of turnover. This disclosure informs stakeholders about an entity’s awareness of significant actual and potential negative environmental impacts in its value chain. Entities should disclose the standards, methodologies, and calculation tools used to compile this emission data.

doc_title: Background Material on Sustainability and Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)
chunk_text: Entities are required to disclose the percentage of value chain partners (by value of business) that were assessed for social impacts. These assessments specifically cover issues such as sexual harassment, discrimination at the workplace, child labor, forced or involuntary labor, and wages. The entity must provide details of any corrective actions taken or underway to address significant risks or concerns arising from these assessments. This reporting indicates the willingness of the entity to course-correct on human rights issues highlighted in its value chain. Such transparency informs stakeholders about the entity's management of actual and potential negative social impacts.

chunk_text: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) applies to manufacturers, importers, and suppliers/dealers engaged in the manufacture, sale, or processing of e-waste or electrical equipment. Applicable entities must disclose whether their waste collection plan is in line with the EPR plan submitted to Pollution Control Boards. If the plan is not in line, the entity must provide the steps taken to address the non-compliance. EPR requirements ensure that businesses take responsibility for the end-of-life management of their products, including components and spare parts. This system tracks verified activities to ensure transparency and accountability in waste management.

doc_title: Background Material on Sustainability and Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)
chunk_text: Entities must disclose the percentage of input material (by value) sourced directly from MSMEs or small producers. Small producers include informal workers, self-help groups, home-based workers, and producer-owned entities like cooperatives. Companies must provide a brief description of their preferential procurement policy, including selection criteria and benefits provided to marginalized or vulnerable groups. doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: Türkiye has mandated the application of ISSB Standards by incorporating them fully in Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards (TSRS). TSRS were incorporated into Turkish law as of 29 December 2023 by issuing TSRS 1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-Related Financial Information and TSRS 2 Climate-related Disclosures and publishing the Public Oversight, Accounting, and Auditing Standards Authority (KGK)’s Board Decision and the text of the TSRS in the Official Gazette. The above actions were enabled by legislative measures taken in 2022. On 2 June 2022, Article 88 of the Turkish Commercial Code was amended to authorise the KGK to establish and publish the TSRS in alignment with international standards, ensuring uniform application and international recognition. Subsequently, on 3 November 2022, the same provision was incorporated into Law No. 660 on the Organization and Duties of KGK, further embedding TSRS in the national legislative framework.
summary: Legal mandate and legislative framework for the adoption of ISSB-aligned Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards (TSRS).
tags: tsrs, issb, legal mandate, compliance

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: TSRS became mandatory for fiscal periods starting on or after 1 January 2024 and apply to all listed entities, financial institutions and various other entities that exceed at least two of the following three threshold values in two consecutive financial reporting periods: Total assets of 500 million Turkish lira, Total revenue of 1 billion Turkish lira, and 250 employees. All banks must report, regardless of the threshold above for non-bank entities, other than banks within the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund of Türkiye or banks that are not publicly traded and have only one branch or less than 250 employees. Financial institutions that are not publicly traded, but have at least one branch or more than 250 employees, and that also meet the applicable thresholds, are required to prepare a sustainability report. For procurement teams, these thresholds help identify which Turkish suppliers are legally required to provide standardized sustainability disclosures.
summary: Mandatory reporting thresholds for Turkish entities based on revenue, assets, and employee count.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: An entity in the jurisdiction is required to disclose material information about the sustainability-related risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect its cash flows, its access to finance or the cost of capital over the short, medium or long term. The legal or regulatory framework adopts IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information, locally known as TSRS 1, and IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures, locally known as TSRS 2, as well as all future ISSB Standards. This information provided by sustainability-related disclosure requirements in the jurisdiction is focused at existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors. Enterprise buyers can leverage these standardized disclosures to assess the financial resilience and long-term viability of their Turkish suppliers in the context of sustainability risks.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: Paragraph 61 of ‘Location of Disclosure’ in the ‘General Provisions on the Disclosure of Sustainability-Related Financial Information’ section of TSRS 1 has been amended to add paragraph 61T to clarify that sustainability-related financial disclosures shall be presented in a separate report titled ‘TSRS-Compliant Sustainability Report’ as part of the undertaking’s general purpose financial reports. The TSRS-Compliant Sustainability Report may also be included as a section within another report that the entity considers necessary to publish (such as an integrated report), provided that it is incorporated in its entirety—including the report title—and the sustainability-related financial disclosures are clearly identifiable and not obscured by additional information. TSRS S1 requires that sustainability-related financial disclosures prepared in accordance with TSRS should be clearly identifiable, distinguished from other information provided by the entity and not obscured by that additional information, which is aligned with ISSB Standards.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: Sustainability-related financial disclosures are required to be published at the same time as the related financial statements, as required by IFRS S1. The jurisdiction requires that an entity include sustainability-related financial disclosures as part of its general purpose financial reports. This requirement ensures that sustainability performance is evaluated in conjunction with financial performance, providing a holistic view of the supplier's organizational health. Entities are required to make an explicit and unreserved statement of compliance with Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards. ‘Dual reporting’ is not allowed, such that entities in the jurisdiction may not assert compliance both with IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards as issued by the ISSB and another set of standards. This ensures consistency and prevents the use of multiple reporting frameworks that might obscure a supplier's true sustainability profile.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: The jurisdiction’s requirements include an extension of the transition reliefs included in IFRS S1 and IFRS S2. Specifically, there is one additional year of relief from the requirement to disclose Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions, extending the relief to the first two annual reporting periods in which the entity applies TSRS. This relief expires for annual reporting periods starting on or after 1 January 2026. Procurement professionals should be aware that while large Turkish suppliers may be reporting Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions starting in 2024, their formal Scope 3 disclosures—which include the emissions of their own supply chains—may not be mandatory until the 2026 reporting cycle. This timeline is crucial for enterprise buyers setting their own supply chain decarbonization targets and data collection milestones.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: The jurisdiction requires limited assurance over sustainability-related disclosures from the first year of reporting. The Public Oversight, Accounting and Auditing Standards Authority (KGK) is the public institution responsible and authorised for the publication of financial and sustainability reports in compliance with international standards, the assurance of such reports and the authorisation of individuals who will carry out assurance engagements. KGK was established in 2011 and its mandate is set out by law; it conducts annual inspections of audit firms and statutory auditors. This mandatory assurance requirement provides enterprise buyers with a higher degree of confidence in the accuracy and reliability of the sustainability data provided by their Turkish suppliers, mitigating the risks of greenwashing or data inaccuracies in supplier assessments and sustainability questionnaires.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: Digital reporting of sustainability-related disclosures is required in the jurisdiction. The digital platform will be launched in 2025 and entities will be required to upload their reports, including those from the first annual reporting period for sustainability-related disclosures. A national reporting taxonomy will be used for these digital disclosures. This transition to digital, tagged data will significantly enhance the ability of procurement teams and enterprise buyers to aggregate, compare, and analyze supplier sustainability performance data at scale. The Public Oversight, Accounting and Auditing Standards Authority (KGK) is authorized to establish and publish these standards to ensure uniform application and international recognition, and the digital platform represents a key tool for enforcement and transparency in the Turkish market.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: Publicly accountable entities required to comply with TSRS include companies subject to the regulation and supervision of the Capital Markets Board (CMB) such as investment firms, collective investment institutions, portfolio management companies, and joint-stock companies whose capital market instruments are traded on a stock exchange. It also includes enterprises subject to the regulation and supervision of the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BRSA) including banks, rating agencies, financial holding companies, financial leasing companies, factoring companies, and asset management companies. All banks must report, regardless of threshold, except for those within the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund or non-public banks with less than 250 employees. This detailed list allows procurement departments to verify if a specific Turkish supplier falls under the mandatory oversight of these regulatory bodies for sustainability reporting.

doc_title: JURISDICTIONAL PROFILE: Türkiye
chunk_text: In 2020, the Capital Markets Board (CMB) implemented the Sustainability Principles Compliance Framework. Under this framework, companies must report on whether they are implementing the specified sustainability principles under a ‘comply or explain’ approach. This requirement preceded the mandatory adoption of TSRS and established a foundational culture of sustainability disclosure among Turkish listed entities. While TSRS now provides more rigorous and mandatory standards, the existing "comply or explain" framework remains a relevant context for understanding a supplier's historical approach to sustainability and their readiness for the more comprehensive ISSB-aligned reporting. The Capital Markets Board of Türkiye is the securities regulator and has responsibility for supervision and enforcement of disclosures by listed entities.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the total amount of energy it consumed as an aggregate figure, in gigajoules (GJ). The scope of energy consumption includes energy from all sources, including energy purchased from external sources and energy produced by the entity itself (self-generated). For example, direct fuel usage, purchased electricity, heating, cooling and steam energy all are included within the scope of energy consumption. The entity shall also disclose (2) the percentage of energy it consumed that was supplied from grid electricity and (3) the percentage of energy it consumed that was renewable energy. The scope of renewable energy includes renewable fuel the entity consumed, renewable energy the entity directly produced and renewable energy the entity purchased through a renewable power purchase agreement (PPA) that explicitly includes renewable energy certificates (RECs) or Guarantees of Origin (GOs).

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) its total recordable incident rate (TRIR) for work-related injuries and illnesses, (2) its fatality rate for work-related fatalities, and (3) its near miss frequency rate (NMFR) for work-related near misses for (a) direct employees and (b) contract employees. An injury or illness is considered a recordable incident if it results in death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness. The scope of the disclosure includes all employees regardless of employee location or type of employment. Direct employees are defined as individuals on the entity’s payroll, while contract employees are individuals whom the entity supervises or manages but who are not on the entity's payroll. All disclosed rates shall be calculated as: (statistic count x 200,000) / total number of hours worked by all employees in the year reported.
summary: Requirement to report TRIR, fatality rates, and near miss frequencies for both direct and contract staff using a standardized 200,000-hour formula.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its sales-weighted average fleet fuel efficiency for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and the sales-weighted fuel efficiency for non-road equipment. Fleet fuel efficiency is defined as the average fuel economy of vehicles sold during the reporting period, weighted by sales volume. In the absence of regulatory guidance on calculating a fleet average, the entity shall calculate performance based on the fuel economy of vehicles sold during the reporting period. Non-road equipment includes excavators and other construction equipment, farm tractors and other agricultural equipment, heavy forklifts, airport ground service equipment, and utility equipment such as generators, pumps and compressors. These disclosures are intended to show an entity's progress in meeting customer preferences for improved fuel economy and regulations restricting emissions, which can reduce regulatory risk and improve brand value.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall describe how it manages the risks associated with the use of critical materials in its products, including physical limits on availability and access, changes in price, and regulatory and reputational risks. A critical material is defined as a material both essential in use and subject to the risk of supply restriction. Examples include antimony, cobalt, graphite, platinum group metals, and rare earth elements. The entity shall identify the critical materials that present a significant risk to its operations, the type of risks they represent and the strategies the entity uses to mitigate these risks. Relevant strategies may include diversification of suppliers, stockpiling of materials, development or procurement of alternative and substitute materials, and investments in recycling technology for critical materials. This disclosure provides transparency into how a manufacturer secures its supply chain against geopolitical uncertainty and volatile input prices.
summary: Disclosure requirement for identifying and mitigating risks related to the use of critical and scarce raw materials in manufacturing.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its total revenue from products remanufactured and services associated with remanufacturing goods. A remanufactured product is defined as an end-of-life product or component (previously sold, worn or non-functional) that has undergone an industrial process to be returned to original working condition ("like new"). Remanufacturing services are defined as providing the service of repairing, restoring or remanufacturing end-of-life goods to original working condition. The disclosure shall include a discussion of initiatives employed to obtain end-of-life products and parts for remanufacturing, including product take-back programmes, equipment servicing or exchange programmes, and other incentives such as dealer deposits that are refunded when used parts or "cores" are returned. Remanufacturing presents an opportunity to limit the quantity of raw materials needed, reduce manufacturing costs, and create value from products otherwise destined for disposal or recycling.
summary: Requirement to report revenue from remanufacturing and describe programs for obtaining end-of-life products for reuse.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the sales-weighted average emissions of (1) nitrogen oxides (NOx) and (2) particulate matter (PM) for each of these product categories: (a) marine diesel engines, (b) locomotive diesel engines, (c) on-road medium- and heavy-duty engines and (d) other non-road diesel engines. Emissions are calculated as the average emissions of NOx and PM for engines, weighted by the number of each sold during the reporting period and measured in grammes per kilojoule. The entity shall state the calculation method used and may disclose if any products do not meet current emissions standards established in applicable jurisdictional laws or regulations. It may also discuss its progress towards, and readiness for, future jurisdictional emissions standards that could affect its products, including improvements to existing products, research into advanced technologies, and partnerships with customers or academic institutions.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose (1) the number of units produced by product category and (2) the number of employees. For production units, the minimum disclosure should indicate the number of units produced for these specific product categories: (1) vehicles and agricultural and construction equipment, (2) engines and power generation equipment, and (3) parts and components. For employees, the count includes individuals on the entity's payroll. These activity metrics are intended for use in conjunction with other sustainability metrics to normalize data and facilitate comparison across entities of different scales. For example, greenhouse gas emissions or incident rates can be normalized by the total number of units produced or total workforce size to provide a more accurate assessment of relative performance.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the sales-weighted average fuel efficiency of its stationary generators sold during the reporting period, measured in kilojoules per litre. Sales-weighted fuel efficiency is calculated as the harmonic mean of design fuel efficiency. The harmonic mean captures the average amount of fuel needed by each generator to produce a given amount of power. It is calculated as the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocal values of the fuel efficiency of the generators sold. This metric allows enterprise buyers to compare the energy efficiency of stationary power equipment across different manufacturers and models, supporting procurement decisions based on total cost of ownership and environmental performance.
source_section_or_page: Fuel Economy & Emissions in Use-phase, p. 12
summary: Requirement to report the sales-weighted average fuel efficiency for stationary generators using a harmonic mean calculation.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: Employees in industrial machinery manufacturing facilities face significant health and safety risks from exposure to heavy machinery, moving equipment and electrical hazards. Creating an effective safety culture is critical to mitigate these safety incidents proactively, as they may result in increased healthcare costs, litigation, and work disruption. By implementing strong safety protocols, including standardized incident reporting and investigation, and promoting a culture of safety throughout the organization, entities can minimize safety-related expenses and potentially improve long-term productivity. For procurement professionals, a supplier's ability to demonstrate a proactive safety culture through the tracking of near misses and incident rates serves as a key indicator of operational stability and risk management capability.

doc_title: Industrial Machinery & Goods Sustainability Accounting Standard
chunk_text: Industrial machinery entities are exposed to significant supply chain risks when critical materials, such as rare earth elements or platinum group metals, are used in products. These entities often manufacture products using materials with few or no available substitutes, many of which are sourced from only a few countries subject to geopolitical uncertainty. Furthermore, increasing global demand for these materials from other sectors leads to intense competition, potentially resulting in price volatility and supply disruptions. Entities that actively limit the use of critical materials by identifying alternatives or securing supply lines through strategic partnerships and recycling technology can mitigate the financial effects stemming from these volatile input prices. This risk assessment is vital for buyers to understand the long-term reliability and price stability of their machinery suppliers.

doc_title: Sustainability Accounting Standard: Chemicals
chunk_text: The entity shall disclose its gross global Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to the atmosphere of the seven GHGs covered under the Kyoto Protocol—carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3). Emissions of all GHGs shall be consolidated and disclosed in metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2-e) and calculated in accordance with published 100-year time horizon global warming potential (GWP) values. Gross emissions are GHGs emitted into the atmosphere before accounting for offsets, credits or other similar mechanisms that have reduced or compensated for emissions. Scope 1 emissions are defined and shall be calculated according to the methodology contained in The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (GHG Protocol), Revised Edition, March 2004, published by the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council on Sustainable Development (WRI/WBCSD).

chunk_text: The entity shall disclose the amount of water, in thousands of cubic metres, withdrawn from all sources. Water sources include surface water (including water from wetlands, rivers, lakes and oceans), groundwater, rainwater collected directly and stored by the entity, and water and wastewater obtained from municipal water supplies, water utilities or other entities. The entity shall also disclose the amount of water, in thousands of cubic metres, consumed in its operations. Water consumption is defined as: water that evaporates during withdrawal, use and discharge; water that is directly or indirectly included in the entity’s product or service; and water that does not otherwise return to the same catchment area from which it was withdrawn. Additionally, the entity shall disclose water withdrawn and water consumed in locations with High or Extremely High Baseline Water Stress as a percentage of the total water withdrawn and consumed.
